--- title: "Lesson 19 · Bayesian thinking: from Bayes' rule to a model equation" subtitle: "Part V · Bayesian modeling" description: "Bayes' rule for a parameter, conjugate updating, how the model equation builds the likelihood, prior × likelihood = posterior, posterior draws, and credible intervals." --- ::: {.meta-pills} [About 3 hours]{} [Before this: Lessons 2, 5 and 8]{} [Threads: likelihood · uncertainty · frequentist ↔ Bayesian]{} ::: ::: {.objectives} By the end of this lesson you will be able to - apply Bayes' rule to a parameter, and update a prior for a risk with data; - explain how a regression's model equation, plus a distribution, builds the likelihood; - describe the prior and the posterior as distributions over the parameters of the model equation; - turn posterior draws back into fitted curves and answers to questions; - interpret a credible interval, and say when it differs from a confidence interval. ::: ::: {.why} **Why it matters.** Bayesian analysis is often presented as a different kind of statistics. It isn't: it uses the same model equations and the same likelihood as the models in Parts II–IV. What it adds is a prior, and a different answer: not one best estimate, but a whole distribution of plausible parameter values. This lesson connects the two views step by step. ::: ## 19.1 Bayes' rule for a risk {#s1} Lesson 2 used Bayes' rule to update the probability of asthma after a test result. Here it updates beliefs about a **parameter**: the risk of asthma by age 8. Start from a **prior** distribution, observe some children, and get a **posterior**. With a beta prior and binomial data, the posterior is also a beta distribution, so the update is simple arithmetic: add the cases and non-cases to the prior's counts. ```{=html}
priorlikelihood (scaled)posterior
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$\pi \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b), \qquad d \mid \pi \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n, \pi)$$ $$\pi \mid d \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a + d,\ b + n - d)$$ ::: {.note} $a + b$ is the prior's strength in "equivalent children"; $a/(a+b)$ its mean. ::: :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r d ~ binomial(n, p) p ~ beta(a, b) a_post <- a + d; b_post <- b + n - d qbeta(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), a_post, b_post) ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#bReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false" title="R code (optional): conjugate updating and a grid posterior"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(19) smp <- cohort |> slice_sample(n = 50) d <- sum(smp$asthma); n <- nrow(smp) a <- 2; b <- 18 # prior mean 10%, worth 20 children # exact conjugate answer qbeta(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), a + d, b + n - d) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 0.1156036 0.1971324 0.3006042 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # the same posterior by brute force on a grid: prior x likelihood, rescaled grid <- tibble(p = seq(0.001, 0.999, by = 0.001)) |> mutate(prior = dbeta(p, a, b), lik = dbinom(d, n, p), post = prior * lik / sum(prior * lik)) grid |> summarise(mean = sum(p * post), low = p[which(cumsum(post) >= 0.025)[1]], high = p[which(cumsum(post) >= 0.975)[1]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> mean low high #> #> 1 0.2 0.116 0.301 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @greenland2006bayesian introduces Bayesian methods for epidemiologists; @gelman2013bayesian chapter-length treatments of conjugate models; @spiegelhalter2004bayesian on priors as "equivalent data" in health research. ::: ## 19.2 The model equation builds the likelihood {#s2} Now a regression. On summer days (June to August), how do emergency visits by Lakeside's older residents depend on temperature? The **model equation** gives each day's expected count from two parameters, α and β; the **Poisson distribution** turns that expectation into a probability for the count that actually happened. Multiply over days and you have the **likelihood** of that pair (α, β). Do it for every pair and you get a likelihood **map**. Click anywhere on it. ```{=html}

Across: β, the effect per °C. Up: the expected visits at 20°C, eα. Darker = more likely. The ring marks your choice.

``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$y_t \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_t), \qquad \log\mu_t = \alpha + \beta\,(T_t - 20)$$ $$L(\alpha, \beta) = \prod_t \frac{\mu_t^{y_t} e^{-\mu_t}}{y_t!}$$ :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r visits[t] ~ poisson(mu[t]) log(mu[t]) = a + b * (temp[t] - 20) loglik <- function(a, b) sum(dpois(d$visits, exp(a + b * (d$temp - 20)), log = TRUE)) ``` :::: ::::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @mcelreath2020statistical builds Bayesian models from the model equation upward; @pawitan2001all on the likelihood as the shared ingredient; @held2020applied on likelihood and Bayesian inference together. ::: ## 19.3 Multiply by the prior: the posterior map {#s3} The **prior** is another map over the same (α, β) plane: how plausible each version of the equation seemed before the data. The **posterior** is the two maps multiplied point by point, then rescaled. That is all "likelihood × prior" means. Try a narrow prior centered on zero (a skeptic), then a narrow prior centered on a large effect, then add more days. ```{=html}

Prior

× Likelihood

= Posterior

``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$p(\alpha, \beta \mid y) \propto p(y \mid \alpha, \beta)\; p(\alpha)\, p(\beta)$$ $$\beta \sim \mathrm{Normal}(m, s^2), \qquad \alpha \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\log 8, 1)$$ :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r visits[t] ~ poisson(mu[t]) log(mu[t]) = a + b * (temp[t] - 20) a ~ normal(log(8), 1) b ~ normal(0, 0.03) brms::brm(visits ~ I(temp - 20), family = poisson, prior = c(prior(normal(2.08, 1), class = Intercept), prior(normal(0, 0.03), class = b)), data = d) ``` :::: ::::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @gelman2013bayesian on posterior computation by grid and simulation; @mcelreath2020statistical on grid approximation as a teaching device; @greenland2006bayesian on priors in epidemiological analysis. ::: ## 19.4 Back to the equation: posterior draws {#s4} Draw points from the posterior map, as MCMC does in practice, and plug each one into the model equation. Each draw gives one curve. The bundle of curves **is** the Bayesian answer, expressed in the language of the model. Any question, such as the effect per °C, the expected visits on a 30°C day, or the probability that heat increases visits, is answered by computing it on every draw. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$(\alpha^{(s)}, \beta^{(s)}) \sim p(\alpha, \beta \mid y), \quad s = 1, \dots, S$$ $$\text{95\% credible interval for } \beta: \ \big[\beta_{(0.025)},\ \beta_{(0.975)}\big]$$ :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit) quantile(draws$b_ItempM20, c(.025, .5, .975)) mean(draws$b_ItempM20 > 0) # P(heat harmful) mean(exp(draws$b_Intercept + 10 * draws$b_ItempM20)) # visits at 30°C ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#dReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Common pitfall"} Thinking a Bayesian model has a different equation from the frequentist one. The model equation and the likelihood are the same; the prior is the only new ingredient. With plenty of data and a weakly informative prior, the posterior median and credible interval closely match the maximum likelihood estimate and the confidence interval. The interpretation is what differs. ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @gelman2013bayesian on summarizing posterior simulations; @kruschke2015doing on credible intervals and posterior probabilities; @bland1998bayesians on Bayesian and frequentist interpretations side by side. ::: ## Check your understanding {#quiz} ```{=html}
``` ## Key takeaways {#take} - Bayes' rule for a parameter: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. With a beta prior and binomial data, the update just adds counts. - The model equation, plus a distribution for the outcome, builds the likelihood. Prior and posterior are distributions over the equation's parameters. - Multiplying prior and likelihood point by point gives the posterior; it lies between them, closer to whichever is more precise. - Posterior draws, plugged into the model equation, give a bundle of curves; any question is answered by computing on the draws. - A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with 95% posterior probability, given the model, prior and data. ```{=html}
